summary: Interpreted the quantified impact receipt (911dce1c4a2849d4a868d72c50403c78, exit 0, both cases passed): all five comparisons are complete and hold, so the replay effect and its cost are decided — one identical TimeoutNow payload honoured a second time raised the term (3 -> 4), one client write out of 138 attempts was refused with 'node is not the leader' at the first step (refusal window shorter than one 10 ms step), one sample in 138 showed no leader, and the control's plain campaign stayed refused with no leadership change. That account is recorded with all three receipts cited, keeping the bounded impact and the unchanged leader identity explicit. While reading further I also traced the network transport's heartbeat fast path: it calls the raft handler inline on the connection goroutine (net_transport.go 721-727), applies only to pure heartbeats (whose request carries no previous entry and no commit index), and therefore touches only lock-protected or atomic state — so the concurrency concern is narrower than the two contradictory comments (api.go 625-632 versus raft.go 1433-1436) suggest. The remaining question in those paths is registered as @q_stale_heartbeat_stepdown with a source-based, unresolved account: appendEntries moves any non-follower to Follower and adopts the message's term whenever the term is greater or the node is not already a follower, so a stale leader's heartbeat could depose the current leader and persist a lower term; its discriminator is a three-voter cluster with two leaders of different terms that can still exchange heartbeats, recorded as the next step. No experiment was requested this turn; the stale-heartbeat probe, delayed delivery variants and larger clusters remain open.
